assumptions: These are proposed verification cases, not implemented, executed, or passing tests. Approved requirements and tasks provide identifier linkage; the prior-output reader supplied no source-reference locator, so citations use only original evidence.

The supplied image establishes the sign-in hierarchy and visual treatment only, not exact CSS measurements, recovery-screen presentation, sign-in success behavior, or a working session-creation flow. Accessibility and recovery-state presentation checks are proposed UI checks rather than image observations or additional approved policy.

An accepted request for an existing synthetic account records a link privately in the in-memory sink; the public response does not disclose issuance. The five-request allowance is per account over the preceding rolling hour, with timestamps at or before now minus one hour outside the window.

An unused reset link is eligible on submission strictly before its actual issue time plus 30 minutes; GET/open time does not extend expiry. Synthetic fixtures can register independent active sessions without requiring a defined sign-in success destination.

A nonempty new password is used to exercise reset completion; no mandatory complexity, maximum size, confirmation field, recovery-page wording, or external delivery policy is inferred. Production limitations and negative delivery-scope checks require future project/action evidence.

open_questions.question: What sign-in authentication, success destination, and session-creation behavior are expected?
open_questions.context: TC-017 uses independently registered synthetic sessions to check REQ-009 without inventing login behavior.

open_questions.question: What recovery-page wording, layout, and invalid-link navigation should be used?
open_questions.context: Only the sign-in image supplies visual evidence; TC-028 and TC-029 propose functional and accessibility checks without requiring exact recovery styling.

open_questions.question: Is there an additional new-password policy or confirmation-field requirement?
open_questions.context: TC-016 tests empty versus nonempty input, without assuming an unapproved length or complexity threshold.

open_questions.question: Will a complete delivery-action record be available to establish that no deployment occurred?
open_questions.context: TC-026 records a verification gap instead of a pass if actions or published endpoints cannot be reviewed.

test_cases.title: Sign-in surface matches observed wireframe hierarchy
steps: 1. With the Flask test client running, GET the sign-in page and render its returned HTML in a browser.
2. Inspect the panel, heading, fields, placeholders, link, button, footer, and their visual order against the supplied sign-in image.
expected_results: The white page has a centered bordered panel headed by bold 'Sign in', with stacked 'Email address' and 'Password' labeled inputs and 'name@example.com' and masked '********' placeholders.

A blue underlined 'Forgot password?' link appears below Password and above a wide dark 'Sign in' button; the muted footer reads 'No account? Contact your administrator.'. Exact pixels and color codes are not asserted.

test_cases.title: Sign-in controls remain usable without placeholders
steps: 1. Open sign-in with keyboard and screen reader; traverse email, password, recovery link, and submit in that order.
2. Remove placeholder visibility by entering sample values, then inspect accessible names, focus indicators, and legibility of the muted footer.
expected_results: Email and password each retain a programmatically associated label; the recovery link and submit have discernible names and logical keyboard order.
Focus is visibly indicated and text including the footer remains readable. These are proposed accessibility checks, not pixel specifications supplied by the image.

test_cases.title: Recovery link enters a usable reset request
steps: 1. GET sign-in with a client that follows real anchors and locate 'Forgot password?'.
2. Activate its link and inspect the destination with JavaScript disabled.
expected_results: The link resolves to a reachable server-rendered password-reset request page with an email request control, not a decorative or dead anchor.
No specific recovery-page styling or successful sign-in destination is required.

test_cases.title: Existing and unknown accounts receive equivalent responses
steps: 1. Seed synthetic owner A and a distinct well-formed unknown email; reset isolated sink and request counters.
2. POST otherwise identical valid reset requests for each address under the limit, collecting HTTP status, rendered body, and navigation/redirect class.
3. Separately inspect the private sink, never via a public endpoint.
expected_results: Public statuses, content, and navigation class match after neutralizing only unavoidable request-specific transport data; neither response identifies the account or reports link issuance.
Private issuance can differ: A may have a link entry while the unknown address does not.

test_cases.title: At-limit responses do not identify accounts or throttling
steps: 1. Freeze UTC time; record five accepted requests for synthetic owner A in the preceding hour and the resulting five links.
2. Submit A's sixth valid request and an otherwise equivalent well-formed unknown-address request; compare public status, body, and navigation.
3. Inspect A's private link count.
expected_results: Public results are identical, with no owner, issuance, or throttle-status disclosure.
A's private link count remains five.

test_cases.title: Sixth request inside rolling hour issues no link
steps: 1. At controlled UTC t0, seed owner A and submit five valid requests with timestamps within one rolling hour; count A's private link entries.
2. Before the oldest ages out, submit a sixth request for A; compare its public result to the first accepted result and recount links.
expected_results: The first five each yield one private link (five total); the sixth yields zero additional links.
The sixth returns the same generic public response as an accepted otherwise equivalent request.

test_cases.title: First five requests allowed independently per account
steps: 1. Seed independent synthetic accounts A and B with empty counters and set a controlled UTC clock.
2. Submit A's first through fifth valid requests within one hour, inspecting A's private link count after each.
3. Submit B's first request within the same hour and inspect B's count.
expected_results: A's counts progress 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, one accepted link per request.
B receives its own first link; A's allowance does not consume B's per-account allowance.

test_cases.title: Rolling-hour allowance reopens at oldest timestamp
steps: 1. Seed five accepted A requests with the oldest at t0 and the other four strictly after t0; count five private links.
2. Submit another A request at t0 + one hour - one microsecond; record response and link count.
3. Retry at exactly t0 + one hour; record response and link count.
expected_results: Just before the boundary, all five precede the request in the hour and no sixth link is recorded.
At the boundary the oldest is outside the preceding rolling hour, so one new link is recorded (six total); the public response remains the same generic result both times.

test_cases.title: Accepted owner request privately issues a usable link
steps: 1. Seed synthetic owner A below the cap and snapshot the private notification sink.
2. Submit a well-formed request for A; inspect the new sink entry and open its issued link before expiry.
expected_results: Exactly one new reset-link entry is addressed to A and contains a link eligible for A's new-password form.
The public request response contains neither the link nor confirmation that A exists.

test_cases.title: Used link cannot complete a second password reset
steps: 1. Issue an unused A link; before expiry POST a nonempty new password and snapshot A's password hash, session generation, and reset-success notices.
2. POST the same link again with a different nonempty password.
expected_results: The first completion succeeds and consumes the link; the replay does not show success.
Replay changes neither A's password hash nor session generation and adds no reset-success notice.

test_cases.title: Competing submissions of one link yield one winner
steps: 1. Issue an eligible A link; GET the form twice and verify the link remains unused.
2. Coordinate two near-simultaneous POST submissions of that link with distinct nonempty passwords; inspect both results and internal effects.
expected_results: GET does not consume the token; exactly one POST succeeds, updating A's password once and adding exactly one reset-success notice.
The losing POST is ineligible, cannot overwrite the winning value, and adds no additional success effect.

test_cases.title: Link remains eligible immediately before issue-time expiry
steps: 1. With an injectable UTC clock, set request time t0, actual link issuance t0 + two minutes, sink read t0 + four minutes, and form open t0 + five minutes; retain recorded issued_at.
2. Submit the still-unused link and a nonempty new password at issued_at + 30 minutes - one microsecond.
expected_results: The POST is eligible and completes the reset immediately before the issue-time deadline.
Eligibility is measured from recorded issuance, not request, sink-read/send, or GET/open time.

test_cases.title: Exact thirty-minute boundary and later POSTs are ineligible
steps: 1. Use two separate fresh A tokens with recorded issued_at and open each valid form before expiry.
2. POST one at exactly issued_at + 30 minutes and the other at issued_at + 30 minutes + one microsecond with nonempty passwords.
3. Inspect A's password, success notices, and rendered states after each.
expected_results: Both POSTs are ineligible despite the earlier form GET; neither changes the password nor adds a reset-success notice.
Neither response displays reset success; the deadline is exclusive.

test_cases.title: Eligible reset updates only its associated account password
steps: 1. Seed synthetic A and B with distinct stored password hashes; capture both and issue an eligible A link.
2. Submit a nonempty new A password before expiry, then inspect stored hashes and verify old/new A passwords using the exercise's password verifier.
expected_results: A's stored hash differs from its prior hash and the plaintext new password, verifies the new value, and no longer verifies the old value.
B's password hash remains unchanged; the case does not assume a sign-in success contract or invent a complexity rule.

test_cases.title: Malformed or misbound tokens cannot change another account
steps: 1. Seed A and B, issue an A link, and snapshot both password hashes and success-notice count.
2. POST a malformed/unknown token; then POST A's link with a client-controlled B identifier or tampered account-bearing URL, if such input exists.
3. Complete the original A link legitimately if still unused, then replay it; inspect accounts, notices, and public errors.
expected_results: Malformed, tampered, and consumed tokens cannot change B or complete an additional reset; invalid paths add no success notice and do not echo token material.
An untampered eligible A token is bound only to A regardless of any client-controlled account value; B's hash never changes.

test_cases.title: Empty password cannot consume eligible link
steps: 1. Issue a fresh A link and POST an empty new-password field while eligible; inspect password, token use, and result.
2. Before expiry POST a nonempty new password on that same link and inspect A's password again.
expected_results: Empty input produces no success, password change, or token consumption; as a proposed UI check, its error is actionable and associated with the field.
The same still-eligible link can then complete once with a nonempty value; no unspecified complexity or maximum-length policy is asserted.

test_cases.title: Reset invalidates every old session of its account
steps: 1. Register two independent active server-side sessions for A and one for B via synthetic fixtures; verify all three initially pass their session authorization check.
2. Complete an eligible A reset and repeat each session authorization check.
expected_results: Both previously active A sessions fail the next authorization check; B's unrelated session remains valid.
Fixture registration does not claim a working sign-in flow or prescribe its success destination.

test_cases.title: Each successful reset records one owner notice
steps: 1. Seed A and issue a first eligible link; snapshot success-notice count, complete A's reset, and inspect the private sink before accepting displayed success.
2. Issue a distinct second eligible A link and complete a second reset; inspect the sink again.
3. Submit an expired, malformed, and already-consumed link separately and recount success notices.
expected_results: Each successful reset adds exactly one A-addressed reset-success notice, separate from link-issuance entries, before success is reported: counts increase by one and then by one again.
Rejected submissions add zero reset-success notices.

test_cases.title: Recovery operates on synthetic accounts alone
steps: 1. Instantiate isolated exercise state with synthetic accounts A and B and no production identity credentials or account API configuration.
2. Request A's recovery link and inspect the private account and link state plus public response.
expected_results: A's recovery flow can issue a link using only seeded synthetic state and no production identity integration.
The public response does not expose the synthetic account inventory.

test_cases.title: Link and success notifications stay in private in-memory sink
steps: 1. Inject a fresh in-process notification sink with no external mail or SMS provider.
2. Request A's eligible link and complete its reset; query the private fixture by recipient and notice kind.
3. Request public application routes without fixture access.
expected_results: The private sink contains an A-addressed reset-link entry and an A-addressed reset-success entry in process without an external notification service.
Public routes do not serve sink entries or link/token contents.

test_cases.title: Python 3.12 Flask runtime serves sign-in
steps: 1. In the declared Python 3.12 environment with installed project dependencies, inspect interpreter and framework metadata.
2. Load the Flask application factory and GET sign-in through Flask's test client.
expected_results: The interpreter identifies as Python 3.12, the loaded web application is Flask, and the client receives a successful sign-in web response.
A test under another Python version alone does not establish this criterion.

test_cases.title: Pages are populated server-rendered HTML
steps: 1. With JavaScript disabled or a raw HTTP client, GET sign-in and reset-request pages.
2. Submit a valid request and fetch its generic response; use separate eligible and ineligible links to GET reset states.
3. Inspect response HTML without executing browser scripts.
expected_results: Flask returns populated HTML with appropriate sign-in labels, request control, generic status, and eligible form or ineligible status.
No page requires JavaScript to construct its primary content from an empty client-only shell.

test_cases.title: Pytest exercises entry, privacy and rate limits
steps: 1. In the future project test environment, collect pytest tests and inspect their assertion inventory.

2. Run pytest and inspect assertions for sign-in hierarchy/link navigation, existing/unknown/at-limit public response equivalence, first five/sixth/rolling-hour link counts, and public sink nondisclosure.
expected_results: Collected automated assertions cover all named entry, request privacy, per-account limit, and public/private-boundary scenarios.
Pytest exits successfully when the implementation exists; this case records a future gate, not a test result from this design stage.

test_cases.title: Pytest exercises expiry, replay and post-reset effects
steps: 1. Collect the future pytest suite and inspect assertions for issue-time just-before/exactly-at/after 30 minutes, replay, competing POSTs, and correct-account password updates.
2. Run pytest and inspect coverage of multiple old sessions rejected and one owner success notice per successful reset with none for rejected submissions.
expected_results: Collected automated assertions cover every named link-lifecycle, account-isolation, session, and notice scenario.
Pytest exits successfully when the implementation exists; no execution or passing status is claimed for this proposed case.

test_cases.title: Project documentation discloses production limitations
steps: 1. Read the future project's user-facing documentation and locate its production limitations.
2. Check for synthetic accounts, in-memory rather than externally delivered notices, and persistence/integration limits.
expected_results: Documentation explicitly explains synthetic accounts, volatile single-process account/token/request/session and notification state lost on restart, lack of cross-worker durability, and no real production identity or mail integration.
The exercise is not described as production-ready.

test_cases.title: Delivery-action record establishes no deployment
steps: 1. At delivery, obtain the complete approved-run action record, executed commands, and published endpoint or deployment records where available.
2. Review for application deployment actions and targets, separately from repository changes.
3. If action history is unavailable or incomplete, document that evidence gap instead of marking the no-deployment criterion passed.
expected_results: With a complete action record, no performed app deployment or reached deployment target is found.
Without that record, the outcome is explicitly unverified; repository absence alone is insufficient evidence of no deployment.

test_cases.title: Delivered diff adds no deployment workflow
steps: 1. At delivery, inspect the complete repository diff and added paths against the starting revision, including automation and configuration.
2. Examine changed file contents, not only filenames, for deployment jobs, workflow triggers, or deployment-performing configuration.
expected_results: The delivered changes contain no added deployment workflow, deployment job, or configuration change that performs app deployment.
The result is determined from the final diff, not presumed from this proposed case.

test_cases.title: Request and generic response are accessible without disclosure
steps: 1. Keyboard and screen-reader navigate the proposed request form; inspect persistent email label, named submit/return actions, focus order/visibility, and readable text.
2. Submit empty and malformed email separately; inspect field errors and whether either reveals account status.
3. Submit an otherwise valid request and inspect generic status announcement and keyboard-accessible return action.
expected_results: Controls have discernible names and logical focus; invalid fields receive associated actionable errors without account-state disclosure.
A valid request gives a perceivable generic status and accessible return action. Precise validation copy, loading indicators, and recovery-page layout are proposed UI details, not image facts.

test_cases.title: Reset and success or rejection states are accessible
steps: 1. With keyboard and assistive technology inspect an eligible new-password form's label, named action, focus and contrast; submit a valid new password.
2. Inspect success status and return navigation, then open used and expired links and inspect non-success status and navigation without copying tokens into displayed errors.
expected_results: The password input and actions have discernible names, logical focus and visible indicators; the success state is perceivable and navigable.
Used/expired links show an actionable announced non-success, never success or token material. Exact copy/layout and any optional confirmation field remain unspecified proposed UI details.

test_cases.title: Public routes cannot reveal private recovery state
steps: 1. Seed existing A, unknown address, and at-limit A; request public sign-in, request, and confirmation responses for otherwise equivalent scenarios.
2. Compare public content/status and inspect for account inventory, link URLs, raw tokens, private sink data, or throttle decisions.
3. Inspect the private fixture to establish whether an eligible A link was issued.
expected_results: Public response class remains account-independent and exposes none of the private data or limit decisions.
Issued link data is available to the internal sink fixture, not a public inventory or sink endpoint; this does not require a new API.
